name: Jaw hammering

lead: Jaw hammering is a variant of bonesmashing: repeatedly striking the jaw with a hammer or another hard object so that, proponents believe, the bone will heal back denser, wider or more angular. The appearance goal is a stronger, more defined jawline and lower face.

The idea circulates in looksmaxxing communities and short video, and is usually justified by the notion that bone adapts to stress. Doctors and surgeons quoted in coverage describe it as misinformation and warn of serious injury.

paras: Accounts describe it only in general terms: hitting the jaw or cheekbone with an object. The wiki does not document techniques. Proponents describe repeated sessions over time and compare it to how bone responds to load.

Wikipedia reports that surgeons warn of fractures, facial misalignment, nerve and blood vessel injuries, deformity and vision changes. Because the jaw carries nerves and teeth, injury can affect chewing, sensation and bite. Anyone with an injury should seek medical care.

angle.text: Practitioners aim for a more angular, defined jaw. The effect is claimed within the community; surgeons describe injury as the documented outcome.

lead: Jaw hammering is a form of bonesmashing in which a person strikes the jaw with a hammer or comparable object, hoping to reshape the lower face. Bonesmashing itself is described by Wikipedia as hitting one's own face with objects [1].

Believers present it as a no-surgery route to a squarer, more prominent jawline: the idea is that bone responds to repeated micro-damage by rebuilding thicker or wider. Wikipedia reports that bonesmashing is rarely practiced and that doctors and surgeons have called it misinformation [1].
No clinical study of the practice exists. Surgeons cited in coverage list fractures, facial misalignment, nerve and blood vessel injury, deformity and vision changes among the risks [1].

paras: Jaw hammering is a regional version of bonesmashing, which targets the cheekbones, jaw and other facial bones [1]. The belief draws on the general idea that bone adapts to mechanical stress.

Wikipedia places looksmaxxing's growth in 2010s online communities and its popularisation on TikTok in the 2020s, with bonesmashing a rarely practiced extreme within it [1]. Media coverage of looksmaxxing in outlets such as the BBC and The Guardian has featured it among the more extreme practices [1].
Doctors and surgeons have criticised bonesmashing, and Wikipedia reports warnings of fractures, facial misalignment, nerve and blood-vessel injury, deformity and vision changes [1].

lore.intro: Bonesmashing in general is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a hardmaxxing extreme [1].

claims.claim: Hitting the jaw makes bone grow back thicker and sharper
